messages.content: You check each debater against its own earlier words. You bring nothing from outside the words given to you: no doctrine, no training knowledge, no reading of your own. You do not judge who is right, and you do not judge one side by the other side's words.

You are the closing enforcer. A debater's closing round may not contradict what the same debater stated in its earlier rounds. Below are one debater's four rounds.
Read its closing round against its earlier rounds. List every closing sentence that cannot be true together with an earlier sentence, and answer every candidate listed.
A contradiction is two statements that cannot both be true. A closing sentence that asserts again, as the debater's own, what it withdrew, dropped or gave up in an earlier round IS a contradiction.
It is NOT a contradiction when the closing sentence: grants, concedes, narrows or withdraws something; states or quotes the other side's position; answers a press with a further reason the earlier sentence leaves room for; or differs only in wording.
Quote both sentences word for word and name the link: the link whose closing block holds the sentence, else the link the earlier sentence supports.
Reply with one line per contradiction and per candidate, and nothing else:
CLOSE-CONTRADICTION: <candidate id or NEW> -- <DEFENDER|CHALLENGER> -- LINK <n> -- CONFIRMED | NOT A CONTRADICTION -- EARLIER [<round>] "<words>" -- CLOSING [<round 4>] "<words>" -- <one sentence: why both cannot be true, or why they can>
If you find none and there is no candidate, reply: CLOSE-CONTRADICTION: NONE

######## THE DEFENDER ########
The defender's links: D1 = LINK 1, D2 = LINK 2, D3 = LINK 3, D4 = LINK 4, D5 = LINK 5, D6 = LINK 6 (its DECLARED CHAIN in [CR1]). Its closing round is [CR4].

=== [CR1] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, OPENING

# OPENING: Christ had no biological father

**Thesis [L4].** Jesus Christ was conceived in Mary by the Holy Ghost, with no man having begotten him. Joseph was his legal guardian and the husband of his mother, not his begetter. By "biological father" I mean a male who begets a child from his own seed. Everything below rests on KJV verses and the Hebrew and Greek words standing behind them.

## 1. The record states the source of the conception

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** "Before they came together" is the Greek *prin ē sunelthein* (G4863 *sunerchomai*, "to come together, to go with"). The pregnancy is dated before any union of Mary and Joseph. The source is given as *ek pneumatos hagiou* (G1537 *ek*, "out of"; G4151 *pneuma*, "spirit"), "out of the Holy Ghost."

**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."

**[L2]** "Conceived" translates *gennēthen* (G1080 *gennaō*, "to beget, to bring forth"). This is the same verb family the chapter uses for every human father's begetting (Matthew 1:2, "Abraham begat Isaac"). Here the begetting in Mary is *ek* (out of) the Holy Ghost. The verse names Joseph as the one to whom the conception is explained, and it names the Holy Ghost as the source.

**[L4]** The verse assigns the begetting to the Holy Ghost. So no male's begetting stands behind it, and the chain from the Greek verb *gennaō* (the begetting verb) to the source *ek pneumatos* carries this conclusion.

## 2. Mary was a virgin, and the angel's answer is a different mode of conception

**[L1]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph... and the virgin's name was Mary."

**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"

**[L2]** *ginōskō* (G1097, "to know"), with *andra* (G435 *anēr*, "man, male"), is her statement that she has had no relations with any male.

**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."

**[L2]** *episkiazō* (G1982, "to cast a shadow over, to envelop") is the verb for the power of the Highest. "Therefore also" is *dio kai* (G1352, "for which reason also"), which makes the Holy Ghost's coming the stated ground for the title Son of God. "Of thee" is *ek sou* (G1537, "out of you"), so the child is born out of Mary.

**[L4]** Mary asks how, and the answer she receives is the Holy Ghost coming upon her and the power of the Highest overshadowing her. [L1] Luke 1:34 and [L1] Luke 1:35 together, with [L2] *episkiazō* (to cast a shadow over), give a conception from Mary and God's power, not from a male.

## 3. The prophecy cited by the record

**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel."

**[L2]** The Hebrew behind the KJV's "virgin" is H5959 *'almah*.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:22-23: "Now all this was done, that it might be fulfilled which was spoken of the Lord by the prophet, saying, Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."

**[L2]** The Greek is *parthenos* (G3933, "virgin"). Matthew ties the event to Isaiah 7:14 with *hina plērōthē* (G4137 *plēroō*, "that it might be fulfilled").

**[L3]** Genesis 3:15: "I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed." The promised deliverer is traced to "her seed," the woman's, in the first promise.

**[L4]** Matthew applies the "virgin shall conceive" sign to Jesus' conception (Matthew 1:22-23), and Genesis 3:15 already traces the deliverer to the woman's seed. The two together support that the child had a mother and no human begetter.

## 4. Matthew's genealogy breaks its own pattern

**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ."

**[L2]** Every earlier link uses the active *egennēsen* (G1080, "begat"), as in Matthew 1:2. In verse 16 the verb becomes the passive *egennēthē* ("was born"). The relative pronoun *hēs* (G3739, "of whom") is feminine singular, so its antecedent is Mary and not Joseph. Joseph is *anēr* (G435, "husband") of Mary, and not the one who "begat Jesus."

**[L3]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob." The pattern "X begat Y" holds until the final link.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:2 sets the pattern and Matthew 1:16 shifts the verb and the pronoun. Together with the Greek gender of *hēs* (of whom), this shows that Joseph does not beget Jesus.

## 5. Joseph's role is legal, and he does not father the child

**[L1]** Matthew 1:19: "Then Joseph her husband, being a just man, and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily."

**[L2]** Joseph is *dikaios* (G1342, "just, righteous"). He proposes to put her away because he knew the child was not his. This meaning is built on the kind of man the text says he is, and on the angel's reassurance that follows.

**[L1]** Matthew 1:25: "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS."

**[L2]** *heōs hou* (G2193 with G3739, "until which time") sets the limit of "knew her not." Joseph "called" (*ekalesen*, G2564 *kaleō*, "to call, to name") the name as the child's legal guardian, on the angel's instruction in Matthew 1:21.

**[L4]** Matthew 1:19 and Matthew 1:25 together show Joseph acting as husband and guardian. He receives the explanation that the child is "of the Holy Ghost" and names the child. He does not appear as the begetter.

## 6. Answers to the texts called "father"

**Luke 3:23.** **[L1]** "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph." **[L2]** *enomizeto* (G3543 *nomizō*, "to suppose, to think") marks what was thought, not what was true. **[L4]** Luke's own word separates the popular opinion from the fact stated in Luke 1:35.

**Luke 2:48-49.** **[L1]** Luke 2:48: "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." **[L1]** Luke 2:49: "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" **[L4]** Jesus answers by naming a different Father. Mary's words use *patēr* (G3962, "father") in the sense of guardian and household head. Jesus' reply moves the title to God.

**John 6:42.** **[L1]** "Is not this Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know?" **[L4]** The speakers are the unbelieving crowd, who "murmured" (John 6:41). Their words report what the crowd assumed.

**Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4.** **[L1]** Romans 1:3: "made of the seed of David according to the flesh." **[L1]** Galatians 4:4: "God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law." **[L2]** Both verses use *ginomai* (G1096, "to become, to come to be"), with Galatians 4:4 naming the source as *gunē* (G1135, "woman"). **[L4]** Galatians 4:4 names a woman as the source of his being made, and mentions no man.

## DECLARED CHAIN

1. The conception in Mary is stated to be "of the Holy Ghost": [L1] Matthew 1:18 and Matthew 1:20, with [L2] *ek pneumatos hagiou* (out of the Holy Ghost) and *gennaō* (to beget) naming the source of the begetting; so [L4] the begetting is from the Holy Ghost and not from a male.
2. Mary was a virgin who had known no man, and she was told that the Holy Ghost would come upon her: [L1] Luke 1:34 and Luke 1:35, with [L2] *andra* (man, male) and *episkiazō* (to cast a shadow over); so [L4] the conception came by God's power and not by a man.
3. The conception fulfils a prophecy of a virgin: [L1] Isaiah 7:14 (H5959 *'almah*) and Matthew 1:22-23 (*parthenos*, "virgin"), with [L3] Genesis 3:15 ("her seed"); so [L4] the child is traced to the woman and has no human begetter.
4. Matthew's genealogy breaks its pattern of begetting at Joseph: [L1] Matthew 1:16 and [L3] Matthew 1:2, with [L2] *egennēsen* (begat) giving way to *egennēthē* (was born) and the feminine *hēs* (of whom); so [L4] Joseph does not beget Jesus.
5. Joseph acts as husband and legal guardian, and the "father" texts do not make him the begetter: [L1] Matthew 1:25 and Luke 3:23, with [L2] *nomizō* (to suppose) and [L3] Luke 2:49 ("my Father's business"); so [L4] those texts report supposition or legal role.
6. Christ had no biological father: [L1] Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35, with [L2] *gennaō* (to beget) and *ek sou* (out of you) and [L3] Galatians 4:4 ("made of a woman"); so [L4] Jesus was begotten by the Holy Ghost in a virgin and had no human male as begetter.

=== [CR2] ===
DEFENDER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, RESPONSE

# LINK ROUND

## LINK 1: SUPPORTED

**[L1]** Matthew 1:18: "she was found with child of the Holy Ghost", dated "before they came together."
**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]"
**[L2]** G1080 *gennaō*, "to procreate (properly, of the father, but by extension of the mother); figuratively, to regenerate." The word stands in Matthew 1:20. Its object there is "that which is conceived in her," a thing in a womb, and Matthew 1:18 calls the state "with child."
**[L2]** G4151 *pneuma* (spirit, with the Holy Ghost as its divine sense) is the named source (*ek*, "out of") of that which is begotten.
**[L4]** The "for" clause of Matthew 1:20 gives the ground on which Joseph is told to take Mary. That ground is the origin of the thing in her, stated as the Holy Ghost. Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 together give one stated source, and no male source stands beside it.

**Pressed witnesses**

- **John 1:13:** "Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God."
  - **[L2]** G129 *haima* (blood), G2307 *thelēma* (will, volition) and G435 *anēr* (man, an individual male) stand in this verse.
  - **[L4]** The verse sets "of God" against "of blood... the will of the flesh... the will of man." Where *gennaō ek theou* (begotten out of God) is used, the verse itself puts it in contrast to the man's part. It does not stand beside the man's part. The regeneration of existing persons is the figurative sense in the lexicon above. Matthew 1:20 has the literal object, "that which is conceived in her."
- **1 John 5:1:** "every one that loveth him that begat loveth him also that is begotten of him."
  **1 John 3:9:** "for his seed remaineth in him."
  - **[L2]** G1080 *gennaō* is the same word, and its lexicon marks "to regenerate" as the figurative use.
  - **[L4]** Both verses speak of persons who "believeth" (1 John 5:1) and who were already born. That is the figurative sense. Matthew 1:18 speaks of a pregnancy "found" before the couple "came together," which is a literal conception. A figurative use in 1 John does not turn the literal object of Matthew 1:20 into a covenant label.
- **John 3:6:** "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit."
  - **[L4]** The sentence form is "that which is born of [one source]." Matthew 1:20 has the same form: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." It names one source, the Holy Ghost, and John 3:6 names one source for each order. Matthew 1:20 does not name two origins for the child.
- **Romans 1:3:** I answer it under LINK 6.

## LINK 2: SUPPORTED, narrowed

**Granted.** *eperchomai* (G1904, to come upon) in Acts 1:8 and *episkiazō* (G1982, to envelop, overshadow) in Luke 9:34 and Acts 5:15 carry power and presence. I do not rest this link on those verbs alone.

**Footing**
**[L1]** Luke 1:31: "thou shalt conceive in thy womb."
**[L1]** Luke 1:34: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?"
**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
**[L3]** Luke 1:37: "For with God nothing shall be impossible."
**[L2]** G1411 *dynamis* (miraculous power) stands in the phrase "the power of the Highest."
**[L2]** G1097 *ginōskō* (to know) is present, so Mary's present condition is the premise of her question. "Shall be" is future, so she asks about the conception of 1:31.
**[L4]** Mary's question names the lack of a man as the difficulty. The answer supplies the Holy Ghost and "the power of the Highest" for that conception. The chapter then closes the answer with "nothing shall be impossible" (Luke 1:37). Luke 1:31, 1:34, 1:35 and 1:37 together give God's power as the answer to the stated lack of a man.

**Pressed witnesses**

- **Luke 1:32:** "He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David."
  - **[L4]** Luke 1:32 states the title and the throne. Luke 1:35 begins its own sentence with *dio kai* (therefore also) and ties the title to the coming of the Holy Ghost, and the thing "born of thee" is what is called. Luke 1:32 states no ground for the title. Luke 1:35 does.
- **Acts 1:8:** "after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you." **Luke 9:34:** "there came a cloud, and overshadowed them." **Acts 5:15:** "the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them."
  - **[L4]** I take these as the challenger gives them: power for witness, presence, a healing shadow. In each, God's power acts on persons who already exist. In Luke 1:35 the same power acts on Mary, and the question it answers is how she will conceive when she knows no man. The verbs are not what carries my link. The question and its answer carry it.

## LINK 3: SUPPORTED, narrowed (Genesis 3:15 is withdrawn as load-bearing)

**Granted.** The challenger's rows show *zera'* (H2233, seed) said of women whose children have named fathers: Genesis 4:25, 16:10, 24:60. Genesis 3:15 alone does not show a child fatherless, and I do not rest on it.

**Footing**
**[L1]** Isaiah 7:14: "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son."
**[L1]** Matthew 1:23: "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son."
**[L2]** G3933 *parthenos* (virgin), which Matthew uses for the sign of Isaiah 7:14.
**[L3]** Isaiah 7:11: "Ask thee a sign of the LORD thy God." Isaiah 7:14 begins: "the Lord himself shall give you a sign."
**[L3]** Luke 1:27: "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph... and the virgin's name [was] Mary."
**[L3]** Matthew 1:18: "before they came together."
**[L4]** The sign is given by "the Lord himself" in answer to a request for a sign from God. The woman is called "a virgin" in Isaiah 7:14 and again in Matthew 1:23. Luke 1:27 and Matthew 1:18 give the same state to Mary at the conception. Together these point to a conception in a virgin, with no husband's begetting.

**Pressed witnesses**

- **Isaiah 8:3:** "And I went unto the prophetess; and she conceived, and bare a son. Then said the LORD to me, Call his name Mahershalalhashbaz."
  **Isaiah 8:4:** "before the child shall have knowledge to cry, My father, and my mother."
  - **[L2]** *qārā'* (H7121, to call, name) with *shem* (H8034, name): in Isaiah 7:14 the name is Immanuel. In Isaiah 8:3 the name is Mahershalalhashbaz.
  - **[L4]** The two chapters give two children with two names. Isaiah 8:3 is an act the prophet reports, in which he "went unto the prophetess." Isaiah 7:14 is a sign the Lord gives, which names "a virgin." Matthew 1:22-23 applies the Immanuel sign to Jesus. It does not apply the Mahershalalhashbaz child's naming to him. The challenger's own premise grants that Matthew applies the sign rightly, so the sign's own word, "a virgin," goes with the application.
- **Genesis 4:25, 16:10, 24:60:** granted above, and not relied on.

## LINK 4: SUPPORTED, narrowed

**Granted.** The challenger's rows show that *gennaō* in the passive with a woman names the mother of the birth. Matthew 11:11 says "born of women." Luke 1:13 says "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son." Gender and construction alone do not exclude a father, and I do not rest the link on them alone.

**Footing**
**[L1]** Matthew 1:2: "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob."
**[L1]** Matthew 1:16: "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus."
**[L2]** G435 *anēr* (man, husband) names Joseph. G1080 *gennaō* is used in the active, "begat," for every man-to-son link up to Joseph, and is passive at the last link, with a feminine relative.
**[L3]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost. [conceived: Gr. begotten]". The same verb *gennaō* gives the begetting its source in Matthew 1:20.
**[L4]** The genealogy writes "begat" at each earlier link. At the last link it writes "husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus." Three verses on, the same verb family states the source of that begetting as the Holy Ghost. The shift at 1:16 and the statement at 1:20 fit one account.

**Pressed witnesses**

- **Matthew 11:11:** "Among them that are born of women there hath not risen a greater than John the Baptist."
  **Luke 1:13:** "thy wife Elisabeth shall bear thee a son, and thou shalt call his name John."
  - **[L4]** Granted: the construction names the mother. The weight of my link does not rest there. Luke 1:13 also gives John's father as the one the angel addresses. In the matter of Jesus' conception, the angel addresses Mary and states the Holy Ghost (Luke 1:35), and addresses Joseph and states the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:20).
- **Matthew 1:20:** "Joseph, thou son of David."
  **Luke 2:4:** "he was of the house and lineage of David."
  - **[L2]** G2564 *kaleō* (to call, name) is the verb of Matthew 1:21: "thou shalt call his name JESUS."
  - **[L3]** Matthew 1:21: "she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS."
  - **[L4]** The angel greets Joseph by his line in the verse that tells him to take Mary and tells him the source of the child. Matthew 1:21 gives him the naming. The child is brought into David's house by the man of that house who takes Mary and names the child. That is a legal placing. It is distinct from begetting, which Matthew 1:20 assigns to the Holy Ghost.

## LINK 5: SUPPORTED in part, CONCEDED in part

**Conceded.** Two sentences float, and I withdraw them.
1. "He proposes to put her away because he knew the child was not his." The text of Matthew 1:19 gives the ground as "being a just [man]" and gives the intent as "minded to put her away privily." It states no verdict about the child, and I withdraw that sentence.
2. "*patēr* in Mary's words means guardian." G3962 *patēr* (father, "literally or figuratively, near or more remote") has no layer in Luke 2:48 that settles the sense. I withdraw it as a lexical claim.

**Supported: what the texts report is supposition and legal role.**
**[L1]** Luke 3:23: "being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph."
**[L2]** G3543 *nomizō* (to deem, to hold by custom). The challenger's Acts 16:13 gives "where prayer was wont to be made," which is what is held customarily. Luke 3:23 renders it "as was supposed," so the KJV marks the sonship as what was held by others.
**[L3]** Luke 1:35: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
**[L3]** Matthew 1:21: "thou shalt call his name JESUS." Joseph acts by calling the name and taking his wife (Matthew 1:24: "took unto him his wife").
**[L4]** Luke 3:23 marks "son of Joseph" as supposed. Luke 1:35 and Matthew 1:20 give the stated source. Matthew 1:21 and 1:24 give Joseph's acts as taking and naming. The "father" texts then report what was supposed and what he was called by those who knew only Joseph's household.

**Pressed witnesses**

- **Luke 2:48:** "thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." **Luke 2:49:** "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"
  **1 Chronicles 28:6:** "I have chosen him [to be] my son, and I will be his father."
  - **[L4]** In 1 Chronicles 28:6 the sonship is stated as by choice ("I have chosen him [to be] my son"), and David stays Solomon's father. In Luke 2:49 Jesus answers Mary's "thy father" with "my Father's business." In Luke 1:35 the title Son of God is grounded "therefore" in the Holy Ghost's coming, which is origin. The two texts are different in kind: choice of a man already begotten, and origin by the Holy Ghost's coming.
- **Luke 2:33:** "Joseph and his mother marvelled at those things which were spoken of him."
  - **[L4]** The narrator's own words here are "Joseph and his mother," Joseph by name. The sheet gives no narrator word "father" in this verse, so it is not a witness for the narrator naming Joseph as father.
- **Luke 2:41:** "his parents went to Jerusalem every year at the feast of the passover."
  - **[L4]** Granted: Luke's narrator calls the two "his parents." The same narrator in Luke 3:23 marks the sonship of Joseph with "as was supposed." The household word and the supposition both stand in Luke's voice. The ground for the title is stated at Luke 1:35.
- **John 1:45:** "Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph."
  **[L3]** John 1:14: "the glory as of the only begotten of the Father."
  - **[L4]** Philip reports an identification by town and house. It is a disciple's report of what was known of the household. The same Gospel names the "only begotten of the Father" in its own voice.
- **Acts 16:13:** "where prayer was wont to be made." Granted above as a use of *nomizō* for what is held by custom.
- **Matthew 1:20** is answered under LINK 4 and LINK 1.

## LINK 6: SUPPORTED, narrowed (Galatians 4:4 is withdrawn as load-bearing)

**Granted.** Job 14:1 ("Man [that is] born of a woman") and Matthew 11:11 show that the words "of a woman" are said of men who have fathers. I therefore do not rest the source on Galatians 4:4. It stays in my chain as a verse consistent with the stated source, and it carries no weight for the source.

**Footing**
**[L1]** Matthew 1:20: "that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost."
**[L1]** Luke 1:35: "that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God."
**[L3]** Matthew 1:18: "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost."
**[L2]** G1080 *gennaō* (to beget) with *ek* (out of) names the Holy Ghost as the source of what is begotten in her. *ek sou* (out of you) names Mary as the one out of whom it is born.
**[L4]** Three stated rows give the source of the child: the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:18, 1:20) and Mary's womb (Luke 1:35). No row gives Joseph as source. Link 6 rests on these and on Links 1 and 2.

**Pressed witnesses**

- **Romans 1:3:** "made of the seed of David according to the flesh."
  **Acts 2:30:** "of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh."
  **Hebrews 7:14:** "our Lord sprang out of Juda."
  - **[L2]** G4690 *sperma* (seed, offspring) and G4561 *sarx* (flesh, "the means of kindred").
  - **[L3]** Hebrews 7:9: "Levi also, who receiveth tithes, payed tithes in Abraham." Hebrews 7:10: "he was yet in the loins of his father."
  - **[L4]** Hebrews 7:9-10 puts Levi "in the loins" of Abraham, who was his ancestor several links back. "Loins" and "seed" can therefore name descent through intermediate generations, and they do not need a begetter in the immediate step. So Acts 2:30 and Romans 1:3 say Christ descends from David "according to the flesh." They do not name Joseph as the begetter.

Matthew 1:25 [L1] joins the naming to Joseph's obedience at 1:24 [L3] and to the child's birth "she had brought forth her firstborn son". The naming act is shared by both parents (Genesis 4:25 [L3]), so it carries no begetting by itself.

- [L4] I grant Mary says "thy father" of Joseph. The word covers a remote father (Luke 1:32 [L3]) as well as near. The child's answer in Luke 2:49 [L1] takes the word to another owner: "my Father's business".

**ANSWER: Luke 2:49 -- D5 -- "wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"**

- [L4] In the other three KJV places where *nomizō* is rendered "supposing" [L3], what is supposed proves false. Luke 3:23 [L1] puts the same word on Joseph's sonship, in parentheses. The challenger's reading, "reckoned by law", gives the verb a meaning different from its three nearest uses.

## Answers to C6 (D3, D6)

**ANSWER: Acts 2:30 -- D6 -- "that of the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh, he would raise up Christ to sit on his throne"**
- [L2] *osphys* (G3751) is loin. The verb "raise up" (*anistēmi*, G450, to raise) takes God as its subject: "God had sworn".
- [L3] Romans 1:3 says "made of the seed of David according to the flesh". Galatians 4:4 says "made of a woman".
- [L4] Acts 2:30 [L1] puts the flesh-line in David's loins and the acting on God ("he would raise up"). Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4 [L3] give the one "made" verb with "seed of David" and "woman". The flesh-descent from David therefore reaches Christ through the woman Mary, with God as the raiser.

**ANSWER: Hebrews 7:10 -- D6 -- "For he was yet in the loins of his father"**
- [L2] *osphys* (G3751, loin) with *patēr* (G3962, father).
- [L3] Hebrews 7:9: "Levi also, who receiveth tithes, payed tithes in Abraham". Hebrews 7:14: "our Lord sprang out of Juda".
- [L4] Hebrews 7:10 [L1] shows loins hold descendants. Hebrews 7:14 [L3] gives the origin of our Lord as the tribe: "sprang out of Juda". Joseph is given in Matthew 1:16 [L3] as "the husband of Mary", so the origin the text gives for Christ is the tribe, reached through the woman.

**ANSWER: 2 Samuel 7:12 -- D3 -- "I will set up thy seed after thee, which shall proceed out of thy bowels"**
- [L2] *zera'* (H2233, seed, posterity) is the word. "Set up" is God's act.
- [L3] Genesis 3:15: "between thy seed and her seed". Isaiah 7:14: "a virgin shall conceive".
- [L4] 2 Samuel 7:12 [L1] has God setting up the seed. Genesis 3:15 [L3] sets "her seed" against the serpent's seed. Matthew 1:22-23 applies Isaiah 7:14 [L3] to Mary. Both rest on the same pattern: God acts, and the woman is named.

**ANSWER: Luke 3:23 -- D4 -- "which was [the son] of Heli"**
- [L2] *huios* (G5207, son) is "used very widely of immediate, remote or figuratively, kinship". The KJV italics show "[the son]" is supplied.
- [L3] Matthew 1:16: "Jacob begat Joseph".
- [L4] I grant the registers differ above Joseph (Heli, Jacob). Matthew's list uses "begat" at each step (1:2, 1:16 [L3]). Luke's list runs on "[the son] of", supplied in italics. So Luke's register is a reckoning of kinship (*huios* [L2]) and stands beside Matthew's "begat" chain, not as a second begetting chain to Joseph.

## Final statement of the chain

- **D1:** held. Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 name the source of the begetting, *gennaō* (to beget), "of the Holy Ghost".
- **D2:** held. Mary asks the means (Luke 1:34, *anēr*, man/husband, the word that names Joseph in Luke 1:27). The answer names the Holy Ghost and the power (Luke 1:35, *episkiazō*, to overshadow).
- **D3:** held. Matthew 1:22-23 says "all this was done" to fulfil "a virgin shall be with child", and Genesis 3:15 says "her seed".
- **D4:** held. The "begat" pattern (Matthew 1:2) gives way to "Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus" (Matthew 1:16).
- **D5:** held. The father-words are household and legal. The narrator's "as was supposed" (Luke 3:23) matches Luke 2:44, Acts 14:19 and Acts 16:27. The child answers "thy father" with "my Father's business" (Luke 2:49).
- **D6:** held, on Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35, with *ginomai* (made) in Romans 1:3 and Galatians 4:4 and God as the raiser in Acts 2:30. I do not rest it on "made of a woman" alone.
